To ask for and take the floor politely: chiedo la parola, se posso aggiungere, mi lasci finire.
To concede a point: glielo concedo, ammettiamo pure che + subjunctive, ha ragione su un punto.
To disagree without aggression: mi permetta di dissentire, non sono affatto d'accordo, la vedo diversamente.
To ask for clarification: che cosa intende per…?, potrebbe essere più preciso?
To summarise the other side's position before replying: se ho capito bene, in altre parole lei sostiene che…
To review the unit: nuanced opinion, formal connectors, the impersonal, the language of debate.

Florence, April, a month before the elections. In the church of Santo Spirito, Mancini is moderating a public debate between the two candidates for the neighbourhood council: Valeria Conti and the lawyer Bardi.
Mr Bardi, you have the floor. You have three minutes.
Thank you. I believe the Oltrarno needs prudence. You can't change the rules every year. You risk scaring off those who invest.
Thank you. Mr Bardi, what exactly do you mean by "prudence"?
I mean not making hasty choices. Letting the market find its balance.
If I have understood correctly, you propose that we do nothing and wait. I grant you that: it's a consistent position. But allow me to disagree.
I didn't say "nothing". I said "with prudence".
Let's assume that's so. The fact remains that, in the last two years, the market has found its balance by closing the haberdashery, the shoemaker's and the bookshop.
I don't agree at all. Those shops closed for many reasons.
Maybe. Then let's do this: the shoemaker is in the hall. Let's give him the floor.
Mr Guido? You have two minutes. Please.
"chiedo la parola" = I ask for the floor
"che cosa intende per" = what do you mean by
"se ho capito bene" = if I have understood correctly
"mi permetta di dissentire" = allow me to disagree
A lei la parola. / Prego, ha tre minuti.
In a public debate, polite formulas are not weakness: they show the audience that you are calm and confident.
Glielo concedo: è una posizione coerente.
Ha ragione su un punto: le regole devono essere chiare.
Non nego che ci siano dei rischi.
"Ammettiamo pure" is a "strategic" concession: you accept the other side's hypothesis only to show that even then they are not right.
Avoid "Lei sbaglia!" or "Non è vero!" in a public debate: it sounds aggressive. Use the formulas above and then the argument.
Se ho capito bene, lei sostiene che…
In altre parole, lei propone di…
"Se ho capito bene" is an elegant weapon: you rephrase the other side's thesis in your own words, showing its weak point, and they must either accept or correct themselves.

The public debate between the candidates for the neighbourhood council took place on a Thursday evening in April, in the church of Santo Spirito. It had been organised by the "Gazzetta dell'Oltrarno", and the priest had agreed on one condition: nobody was allowed to raise their voice under Brunelleschi's dome. Mancini, who was the moderator, had prepared a tomato-shaped kitchen timer, borrowed from Graziella, to control the time of each speech. Three minutes for the opening, two for the rebuttal, one for the conclusion. When the tomato rang, you had to stop talking. Even in the middle of a sentence.

The church was as full as at Christmas Mass. There were residents, shopkeepers, pupils from the San Frediano school with their parents, the angels of the mud who had stayed in touch after the launch of Bellini's book. In the front row sat Guido, the former shoemaker from via Toscanella, in his Sunday jacket. Next to him was Graziella, who had closed the trattoria for an evening, something she hadn't done for years, and who had put a sign on the door: "Closed for democracy". Pietro and Davide were sitting on the altar steps, notebooks in hand, taking notes for the school newspaper.

Before it began, in the sacristy, Valeria was pale. Giulia, who had lived through the same fear on television five months earlier, took her aside. "I'll just tell you what I was told," she said. "You don't have to win. You have to show that you listen. Always concede something before you contradict. And when you don't know what to say, ask the other person what they mean. Usually they don't know either." Valeria laughed nervously. Then Giulia took a cloth handkerchief out of her bag. Inside was Ernesto's tiny brush, which Bellini had lent again, "because it's now the official talisman of every debate in this family". Valeria put it in her jacket pocket without a word.

The lawyer Bardi spoke first. He was an elegant speaker, used to courtrooms, and his speech was built like a Swiss watch. He said he loved the Oltrarno, where his family had lived for three generations. He said that overly rigid rules would scare off those who want to invest in the neighbourhood. He said prudence was needed, balance, respect for the market. He used all the right connectors: "first of all", "on top of that", "nevertheless", "therefore". When the tomato rang, the hall applauded politely. Pietro, on the steps, wrote in his notebook: "He speaks beautifully. But he said nothing."

Davide, beside him, had counted the connectors in Bardi's speech in a corner of his notebook, with little strokes, the way you count points at cards. "Twenty-three," he whispered to Pietro. "In three minutes. More than one every eight seconds." Pietro nodded. "It's like a very beautiful wall," he whispered back, "with perfect stones and perfect cement. But without a door to go in by." Davide looked at him with admiration and wrote the sentence in his notebook, under the strokes. Two weeks later, in the school newspaper, the sentence appeared under the title "The wall without a door", and the Italian teacher read it in every class, without saying who it was about.

Then it was Valeria's turn. She read nothing. In her hand she held only the notebook with the neighbourhood's three hundred and three problems, which she kept closed. "I ask for the floor, if I may," she said, although it was already her turn, and someone in the hall laughed. "Before I speak, I'd like to ask Mr Bardi a question." She turned to Bardi. "Mr Bardi, what exactly do you mean by 'prudence'?" Bardi smiled, like a chess player who had been waiting for that move. "I mean not making hasty choices," he replied. "Letting the market find its natural balance."

"If I have understood correctly," said Valeria calmly, "you propose that we do nothing and wait. I grant you that: it's a consistent position. I don't deny there are risks in changing the rules. But allow me to disagree." She paused, as Bellini had taught Pietro. "Let's assume the market finds a balance. The fact remains that, in the last two years, the market has found its balance by closing the haberdashery in via dei Serragli, the bookshop in via Toscanella and the shoemaker's of the gentleman sitting in the front row. That, to me, is not balance. It is depopulation."

Bardi raised a hand. "I don't agree at all," he said, with a smile that was beginning to stiffen. "Those shops closed for many reasons: the crisis, the internet, the owners' age. You can't blame rents for everything." It was a good argument. In the hall someone nodded. Valeria listened to the end, without interrupting. Then she said something nobody expected. "You may be right," she said. "I'm not a shoemaker, and neither are you. So let's do this. The shoemaker is in the hall. Let's give him the floor. He knows better than we do why he closed."

Mancini looked at the rules, then at the audience, then at the tomato. There was no rule forbidding it. "Mr Guido," he said, "you have two minutes. Please." Guido stood up slowly. He had never spoken in public in his life. He took off his hat, turned it in his hands, and for a moment seemed unable to say anything. Then Graziella, sitting next to him, touched his arm. And Guido spoke. He used no connectors, no polite formulas. He spoke the way you speak at a shop counter, with the simple words of someone who has worked with his hands for fifty years.

"I didn't close because of the internet," he said. "You can't resole shoes on the internet. And I didn't close because of my age: I'm seventy-two and my hands still work very well. I closed because the owner tripled my rent. From six hundred to one thousand eight hundred euros a month. For a twelve-square-metre shop, without a window. In my place there's now a shop selling magnets of Michelangelo's David. David in his underpants, David in sunglasses. With all due respect to Mr Bardi, that isn't the market finding its balance. It's the market finding its tourists."

The church burst into laughter and then applause. Guido waited for it to finish, then added something, more quietly. "And now who repairs Graziella's shoes? I've been doing them for thirty years. They broke again last month, and she's walking around with sticky tape under the sole." Graziella turned as red as Mancini's tomato. The audience laughed again. Guido put his hat back on, sat down, and the tomato rang at exactly that moment, as if it had understood there was nothing more to add.

At that moment, Pietro noticed something nobody else saw. The lawyer Bardi, while Guido was speaking, had lowered his eyes to his own shoes, elegant shoes of English leather, polished to a mirror shine. And when Guido sat down, Bardi leaned towards him, across the candidates' table, and said something quietly. Guido looked at him in surprise, then nodded. Only after the end of the debate did Pietro find out what they had said. Bardi had asked him whether he was the same Guido who, in the eighties, used to repair the shoes of his father, the old notary Bardi, "the one who never paid on time". It was him. And the notary, Guido laughed, still owed him three soles.

Bardi, in his rebuttal, was fair. "I grant you that," he said, addressing Guido. "Your case is unjust. And I don't deny there are others like it. However, the solution cannot be to force owners to do charity." It was a good answer, and Valeria knew it. In her rebuttal she didn't attack. She only said: "Nobody is asking for charity, Mr Bardi. We're asking for something simpler: that the council use part of the tourists' tourist tax to help historic shops and craftsmen pay their rent. In short: the tourists who come to see the real city help the real city to stay."

In his conclusion, Bardi spoke one last time about prudence, elegantly. Valeria, on the other hand, did something strange. She finally opened the notebook and read, one after another, the first ten problems on the list, with the name of the person who had told them. The broken pavement in front of the school, Rita's. The fruit seller's van. The missing gym. The haberdashery. Guido's rent. Then she closed the notebook. "There are another two hundred and ninety-three," she said. "I won't solve them all. But I know them one by one. And each one has a face." The tomato rang. For ten seconds, in the church, there wasn't a sound. Then the applause.

The elections were held a month later, on the second Sunday in May. Voting took place in a primary school in via della Chiesa, and all day long there was a very long queue in front of the polling station, something which, the neighbourhood's old people said, had never been seen before for a neighbourhood council. Graziella voted at eight in the morning, in her shoes repaired with sticky tape. Efisio and Lucia voted together, holding hands, as at their wedding. Guido voted last, at one minute to ten in the evening, "because you vote calmly, the way you put a sole on a shoe".

Pietro and Davide, who couldn't vote because they were thirteen, spent the day on a bench in front of the polling station, with a thermos of "tea" prepared by Graziella and a sign made by Davide: "We can't vote yet. But we're watching." Every time someone came out from voting, Pietro asked them, with the seriousness of a journalist, whether voting had been easy or hard. The answers went into the black notebook. One lady said she had voted "with her heart". A young man said he had voted "for the first time and didn't know where to put the cross". An old man said only: "I voted. That's more than enough."

The counting of the votes went on until midnight. In the trattoria, everyone was waiting in front of the old television above the counter, where a local channel was giving the results live. But it was Mancini who, in the end, brought the news, running in through the door with his phone in his hand and out of breath. "Elected!" he shouted. "With sixty-two per cent! The most voted in the whole neighbourhood!" The trattoria exploded. Lupino barked. Viola, woken by the noise, came down the stairs in her pyjamas asking if it was Christmas. Valeria, sitting at the table by the window, said nothing. She put her hands over her face and stayed like that for a long time.

The first to congratulate her, the next day, was the lawyer Bardi himself. He came to the trattoria at lunchtime, with a bunch of flowers and his tie slightly loosened, and asked to speak to her. "I lost," he said, shaking her hand. "And I deserved it. You had the faces, I had the formulas." Then he added, in a lower voice: "Allow me to disagree one last time: prudence is useful. But I promise you one thing. On the council, if you propose to help the craftsmen with the tourists' tax, I'll vote in favour. Prudently." Valeria laughed. "I accept," she said. "In fact, I'll put it in writing."

That evening Valeria stopped by the workshop, where Bellini was closing up. She gave him back Ernesto's brush, wrapped in the handkerchief. "It works," she said. "I won." Bellini put it back in the drawer carefully. "It isn't the brush," he replied. "It's that you did what a good restorer does. First you looked. Then you listened. And only at the end did you touch." Valeria thought for a moment. "And now?" she asked. Bellini locked the drawer. "Now comes the hard part," he said. "One millimetre at a time. Five years." Valeria laughed. "I think I'm going to need a lot of ribollita," she said. "So do I," replied Bellini.

Councillor Valeria Conti's first proposal was presented in June, at the first meeting of the neighbourhood council. It was called the "Shops Project" and provided that part of the tourist tax paid by tourists in the Oltrarno be used to help craftsmen reopen in the neighbourhood. It was approved unanimously, with the vote in favour of the lawyer Bardi, who during the discussion asked for the floor only to say: "I grant you that. Prudently." The hall laughed. And the first craftsman to receive the help, in September, was a seventy-two-year-old shoemaker.

Guido's new shop opened on the first Monday in October, in via Maggio, fifty metres from the trattoria, in a small shop that had stood empty for three years. It was even smaller than the one in via Toscanella, but it had a window. Above the door, Davide had hand-painted a sign: "Guido's Shoemaker's — since 1974, again". The first customer, of course, was Graziella, who came in at half past eight with her black shoes wrapped in a sheet of newspaper and put them on the counter without a word. Guido looked at them, removed the sticky tape from the sole delicately, the way you remove a plaster from a child, and shook his head. "Graziella," he said, "these shoes need a restoration, not a repair."

"Then I'll call Bellini," replied Graziella. They both laughed. In front of the shop a small crowd had already gathered: Valeria, Pietro, Davide, the fruit seller with her van parked, at last, without a fine, because that too had been approved by the council, at point number three hundred and two. Mancini took a photo of Guido working on Graziella's shoes and the next day published it on the front page with a two-word headline, chosen by Pietro: "Point three hundred and three." Below, a caption: "Councillor Conti's election programme began with ribollita. A year later, it has reached the shoes of the woman who cooks it."

That evening Pietro wrote in the black notebook, under the date: "Today I understood how democracy works. You ask for the floor. You listen to the other person. You concede what it's fair to concede. You disagree politely. And then, if you're lucky and patient, a shoemaker reopens his shop and Grandma no longer walks around with sticky tape under her shoes." He reread it and thought it was the longest sentence he had ever written. Then he added, underneath: "P.S. Mancini's tomato has gone back to the kitchen. Grandma says that, after all that politics, her sauces come out better."
